hints: Think about what the prefix mono- means compared to poly- and how small building blocks relate to a very long DNA chain.
walkthrough:
Link Mono to Poly**
Think of DNA as a very long chain. That chain is not built in one piece, it is built by joining many small identical-type building blocks end to end. Mono means single or small, poly means many.

Name the Building Block**
For DNA those repeating small molecules are nucleotides. Many nucleotides joined together form the polynucleotide strand, so monomers of DNA means the nucleotides that make up the DNA polymer.
Final answer: Repeating sub-units (nucleotides) used to make a polymer / polynucleotide / strand of DNA.

hints: Look closely at the bottom of the pentose sugar in Fig. 4.1 and compare the two groups shown at the lower carbons, then recall which sugar ATP contains.
walkthrough:
Read the Sugar in Fig. 4.1**
The sugar in the diagram has H on the right-hand lower carbon (C2') and OH on the left. That is deoxyribose, deoxy means missing one oxygen compared to ribose. This is the sugar used for DNA.

Recall the Sugar in ATP**
ATP is a ribonucleotide used as an energy carrier, not a DNA building block. Its sugar is ribose, which has -OH groups on both lower carbons. So at C2, ATP has -OH where Fig. 4.1 has -H.
Final answer: ATP contains ribose (not deoxyribose); the C2 of the pentose has -OH not -H.

hints: Think of the one energy-releasing process that every living cell carries out to make its usable energy currency, whether it photosynthesises or not.
walkthrough:
Identify the Universal ATP Source**
All living cells need to make ATP from ADP and phosphate using energy released from glucose and other substrates. That process is respiration, including glycolysis and aerobic respiration where present.

Avoid the Photosynthesis Trap**
Photosynthesis also makes ATP, but only in some plant and algal cells in light. Respiration is the process occurring in all cells that results in ATP production.

hints: First identify the two base pairs in Fig. 4.2 by base size and shape - the top pair is adenine with thymine and the bottom pair is guanine with cytosine.
Now recall the fixed rule for complementary pairing: think A-T has two shared sites and C-G has three shared sites for hydrogen bonds.
walkthrough:
Match the Bases**
On the right, strand Y top base with the $NH_2$ group is adenine. Opposite it on the left is thymine with two $C=O$ groups and $CH_3$. At the bottom, the right base with two $NH$ groups and one $C=O$ is guanine, opposite cytosine on the left with one $NH_2$ and one $C=O$. So you have A-T on top and G-C below.

Apply the 2-and-3 Rule**
Adenine and thymine always pair with two hydrogen bonds between them. Cytosine and guanine always pair with three hydrogen bonds. Draw two separate dotted lines across the gap for the top A-T pair and three separate dotted lines across the gap for the bottom C-G pair, joining H to N or O atoms.

Final answer: Draw two hydrogen bonds (dotted lines) between A and T in the upper pair and three hydrogen bonds between C and G in the lower pair, correctly positioned between complementary N-H and C=O groups.

hints: Look at what X joins together - a phosphate group bridging the sugars of two adjacent nucleotides in the same strand.
walkthrough:
Locate Bond X**
X labels the linkage between one nucleotide and the next in the same strand, where a single phosphate connects to the sugar above and the $CH_2$-sugar below.

Name the Backbone Bond**
A phosphate joined by two ester links to two sugars is called a phosphodiester bond. It forms the continuous sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA and is made during replication and broken during hydrolysis.
